position_in_era.historical_role: Pre-anchor tritone riff: the opening E–G# tritone (the 'devil's interval' — diabolus in musica — also the core interval of Black Sabbath's self-titled track) delivered as a guitar-first motif before any vocal. Hendrix's use of the tritone and distortion as compositional tools, not decoration, is the direct harmonic precursor to Tony Iommi's approach.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded January 1967 at De Lane Lea Studios, London. Hendrix played a right-handed Fender Stratocaster strung and played left-handed, run through a Marshall stack with Univibe and Octavia effects on the solo. The tritone opening riff — E to B-flat — was described by Hendrix as inspired by a dream about 'walking under a purple haze.' Produced by Chas Chandler.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Hendrix dominates all compositional decisions; Noel Redding (bass) and Mitch Mitchell (drums) serve the riff rather than contest it. Mitchell's jazz-inflected drumming is the only voice that approaches dialogue with Hendrix's guitar rather than pure support.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Hendrix: Fender Stratocaster (left-handed, reversed strings); Marshall 100W stack; Univibe for solo section; Octavia octave-doubler for the solo's upper register. The E–G# tritone interval is the song's harmonic spine.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Released March 1967 as UK single, reached #3. Became the defining document of Hendrix's riff vocabulary. The tritone — historically banned in medieval music as diabolic — reappears three years later as the opening interval of Black Sabbath's self-titled song, consciously chosen by Iommi and Butler for its unsettling quality.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: UK single February 1967; US release on Are You Experienced, August 1967. Hendrix performed the song on Top of the Pops wearing his Army jacket — the image of riff-as-weapon in visual form.
